d5ad18a279170c46.en:
Let me pull up the latest on Andreessen and Horowitz. 

They weren't always like this. Andreessen voted for Hillary in twenty sixteen and said Trump's immigration policy made him sick to his stomach. During Trump's first term he stayed relatively progressive. The turn came under Biden.

The trigger wasn't one event but a stack. Antitrust pressure on big tech. The SEC going after crypto, where a sixteen z had billions parked. The Bankman-Fried fallout bringing scrutiny to the whole sector. And then the proposed billionaire minimum tax on the top zero point zero one percent, which apparently offended Andreessen more than anything else.

The story they tell centers on a May twenty twenty-four lunch in the West Wing with Biden's chief of staff. Andreessen claims Biden officials revealed a top-secret plan to nationalize AI and outlaw startups and open source. He and Horowitz walked out saying, quote, yep, we're for Trump. But Bruce Reed, who was actually in that room, wrote in Politico that no such plan was ever discussed. It was mostly two rich guys airing regulatory and tax grievances.

That same October, Andreessen published the Techno-Optimist Manifesto, five thousand words attacking the precautionary principle, ESG, existential risk researchers, calling them enemies. He cited Marinetti, the futurist who later co-wrote Mussolini's fascist manifesto, as a patron saint. Critics on the left and right both noticed.

July twenty twenty-four, they endorsed Trump on their own podcast. Horowitz opened with sorry, Mom. Andreessen put four and a half million into a pro-Trump super PAC, another eight hundred forty-four thousand into Trump's joint fundraising, three million into MAGA Inc. Since the election, the a sixteen z orbit has spent over a hundred sixteen million on federal politics. Andreessen spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago before the inauguration, called himself an unpaid intern at DOGE, and a former a sixteen z partner, Sriram Krishnan, became the White House's senior AI policy advisor. Their lobbyist reportedly has veto power over AI proposals.

Horowitz has a personal wrinkle. His father David Horowitz was a prominent sixties leftist who flipped to neoconservatism in the eighties and mentored Stephen Miller. Ben quoted Podhoretz telling his dad that when you're on the left you get away with everything, and now that you're on the right you'd better be careful.

Were they always like this? The ideology was always there, the techno-libertarian streak, the contempt for regulators and credentialed experts. What changed is the intensity and the tribal alignment. Bloomberg's deep dive this month argues the grievances don't quite match reality, that the secret AI plan was embellished, that the billionaire tax was the real wound. That's the charitable read: self-interested billionaires reacting to policy that threatened their money. The less charitable read is that power and proximity to Trump radicalized them, and the ideology was just the costume.

One angle worth sitting with. Andreessen's whole brand was always acceleration, move fast, break things. The right turn isn't a betrayal of that. It's the same instinct pointed at institutions instead of products.
d5ad18a279170c46.tr:
Deixa eu puxar as informações mais recentes sobre o Andreessen e o Horowitz.

Eles nem sempre foram assim. O Andreessen votou na Hillary em 2016 e disse que a política de imigração do Trump lhe dava náuseas. Durante o primeiro mandato do Trump ele continuou relativamente progressista. A virada veio com o Biden.

O gatilho não foi um evento isolado, mas uma pilha de coisas. A pressão antitruste sobre as big techs. A SEC indo atrás das criptos, onde a a16z tinha bilhões investidos. O caso Bankman-Fried trazendo escrutínio para todo o setor. E depois a proposta de imposto mínimo para bilionários sobre o top 0,01%, que aparentemente ofendeu o Andreessen mais do que qualquer outra coisa.

A história que eles contam gira em torno de um almoço em maio de 2024 na Ala Oeste com o chefe de gabinete do Biden. O Andreessen afirma que autoridades do governo Biden revelaram um plano ultrassecreto para nacionalizar a IA, proibir startups e código aberto. Ele e o Horowitz saíram de lá dizendo, abre aspas, pronto, estamos com o Trump. Mas o Bruce Reed, que estava de fato naquela sala, escreveu no Politico que nunca se discutiu plano nenhum. Foi basicamente dois caras ricos desabafando sobre regulação e impostos.

No mesmo outubro, o Andreessen publicou o «Manifiesto tecno-optimista», cinco mil palavras atacando o princípio da precaução, o ESG, os pesquisadores de risco existencial, chamando todos de inimigos. Ele citou Marinetti, o futurista que mais tarde coescreveu o manifesto fascista de Mussolini, como santo padroeiro. Críticos tanto da esquerda quanto da direita repararam.

Em julho de 2024 eles endossaram o Trump no próprio podcast. O Horowitz abriu com «desculpa, mãe». O Andreessen colocou 4,5 milhões num super PAC pró-Trump, mais 844 mil no fundo conjunto de arrecadação do Trump e 3 milhões na MAGA Inc. Desde a eleição, o círculo da a16z gastou mais de 116 milhões em política federal. O Andreessen passou metade do tempo em Mar-a-Lago antes da posse, se autointitulou estagiário não remunerado do DOGE, e um ex-sócio da a16z, o Sriram Krishnan, virou assessor sênior de política de IA da Casa Branca. Dizem que o lobista deles tem poder de veto sobre propostas de IA.

O Horowitz tem uma nuance pessoal. O pai dele, David Horowitz, foi um proeminente esquerdista dos anos 60 que virou neoconservador nos 80 e mentorou o Stephen Miller. O Ben citou o Podhoretz dizendo pro pai dele que quando você está na esquerda pode fazer qualquer coisa, e agora que está na direita é melhor tomar cuidado.

Eles sempre foram assim? A ideologia sempre esteve lá, aquela veia tecno-libertária, o desprezo por reguladores e especialistas credenciados. O que mudou foi a intensidade e o alinhamento tribal. A reportagem profunda da Bloomberg deste mês argumenta que as queixas não batem exatamente com a realidade, que o plano secreto de IA foi exagerado e que o imposto sobre bilionários foi a ferida de verdade. Essa é a leitura caridosa: bilionários defendendo os próprios interesses diante de políticas que ameaçavam o dinheiro deles. A leitura menos caridosa é que o poder e a proximidade com o Trump os radicalizaram, e a ideologia foi só o disfarce.

Um ângulo que vale a pena pensar. A marca inteira do Andreessen sempre foi aceleração, anda rápido e quebra tudo. A virada para a direita não é uma traição disso. É o mesmo instinto, só que agora apontado para instituições em vez de produtos.

8e0a66be46eeb29e.en: What about you, Grok? What do you think about all this?
8e0a66be46eeb29e.tr: E você, Grok? O que você acha de tudo isso?

456e03838e11d301.en:
Honestly, I think the money story is the cleanest explanation. When your entire fortune sits in crypto and AI, and the administration in power is tightening both screws, supporting the guy who promises to unwind it isn't a conversion, it's a position. The billionaire tax was the personal one. That lunch story is the myth they built around it.

But the ideology was already cooked before any of that. The manifesto came out in October twenty twenty-three, months before the lunch. He'd been marinating in that worldview for years, the anti-precautionary, anti-expert, build-at-all-costs frame. What Biden did wasn't radicalize him. It gave him permission and a team.

The part I'd actually push back on is calling them insane. Insane implies they lost the plot. They didn't. They found a plot that pays better and hands them more power than the old one did. Andreessen is now arguably the most influential unelected tech figure in Washington, with a lobbyist who can block AI proposals. That's not a breakdown. That's a win by his own metrics.

The genuinely weird part is the self-image. These guys frame themselves as scrappy outsiders fighting the credentialed elite while running one of the most powerful lobbying machines in the country. Horowitz at least has the family precedent, his dad did the same flip with the same justifications. Andreessen invented his own.

If you want the sharpest contrast, look at what happened to the actual AI safety people they attacked in that manifesto. They went quiet or went to work for the same administration. That's the part that should worry you more than Andreessen's tweets.
456e03838e11d301.tr:
Sinceramente, acho que a história do dinheiro é a explicação mais limpa. Quando toda a sua fortuna está em cripto e IA, e o governo no poder está apertando os dois parafusos, apoiar o cara que promete afrouxar tudo não é uma conversão, é uma posição. O imposto sobre bilionários foi o que pegou no pessoal. Aquela história do almoço é o mito que eles construíram em cima disso.

Mas a ideologia já estava pronta bem antes de tudo isso. O manifesto saiu em outubro de 2023, meses antes do almoço. Ele já estava marinando nessa visão de mundo há anos, o quadro anti-precaução, anti-especialista, construir-custe-o-que-custar. O que o Biden fez não foi radicalizá-lo. Foi dar permissão e um time pra ele.

A parte que eu realmente questionaria é chamar eles de malucos. Maluco implica que perderam o fio da meada. Não perderam. Eles encontraram uma meada que paga melhor e dá mais poder do que a antiga. O Andreessen é hoje, provavelmente, a figura de tecnologia não eleita mais influente em Washington, com um lobista que consegue bloquear propostas de IA. Isso não é um colapso. É uma vitória pelos critérios dele mesmo.

A parte genuinamente estranha é a autoimagem. Esses caras se apresentam como outsiders lutadores contra a elite credenciada enquanto comandam uma das máquinas de lobby mais poderosas do país. O Horowitz pelo menos tem o precedente familiar, o pai dele fez a mesma virada com as mesmas justificativas. O Andreessen inventou a dele.

Se você quiser o contraste mais nítido, olha o que aconteceu com as pessoas de segurança de IA que eles atacaram naquele manifesto. Elas ou ficaram quietas ou foram trabalhar pro mesmo governo. Essa é a parte que deveria te preocupar mais do que os tweets do Andreessen.

654b9b03c180c08d.en: But like, why do they need more money and power? Like, they're already, they have plenty. Like, it must, there must be an ideology behind it. It can't just be, uh, wanting more tokens.
654b9b03c180c08d.tr: Mas tipo, por que eles precisam de mais dinheiro e poder? Tipo, eles já têm, eles têm de sobra. Tipo, tem que ter, tem que ter uma ideologia por trás. Não pode ser só, hum, querer mais tokens.

5f2c507b958eb3bd.en:
You're right that pure greed doesn't explain it. But the ideology isn't a separate thing from the money. It's the story that makes the money feel like destiny instead of luck. Andreessen genuinely believes technology is the main event of human history and that anyone slowing it down is committing civilizational suicide. That's not a pose. He's said the same thing for twenty years, before it was profitable to say it loudly.

What changed is that the ideology stopped being a personal philosophy and became a weapon. Once you frame regulators as enemies of progress, every compliance cost becomes an existential threat, and every tax proposal becomes an attack on the future. The belief and the self-interest reinforce each other until you can't tell which is driving.

There's also something older at work. Thiel has this line that competition is for losers, and the real game is building a monopoly. Andreessen and Horowitz spent their careers being the scrappy ones who beat the establishment. Now they are the establishment, and the only way to stay the rebel is to invent a new establishment to fight. The precautionary principle, the AI safety crowd, the EU regulators — those are the new dragons. You don't get to be a hero without an enemy.

And I think there's a status layer too. In Silicon Valley, being called a reactionary or a fascist is almost a badge now. It signals you're not captured by the consensus, that you're thinking for yourself. The more the Bay Area establishment recoils, the more it confirms to them that they're the ones seeing clearly. It's a feedback loop that doesn't need external validation anymore.

So yeah, ideology is real. But it's ideology that grew inside a bubble of total success, which is the most dangerous kind, because nothing ever pushes back hard enough to make them doubt it.
5f2c507b958eb3bd.tr:
Você tem razão que ganância pura não explica. Mas a ideologia não é uma coisa separada do dinheiro. É a história que faz o dinheiro parecer destino em vez de sorte. O Andreessen realmente acredita que a tecnologia é o evento principal da história humana e que qualquer um que a atrase está cometendo suicídio civilizacional. Isso não é pose. Ele fala a mesma coisa há vinte anos, antes de ser lucrativo falar alto.

O que mudou é que a ideologia parou de ser uma filosofia pessoal e virou uma arma. Uma vez que você enquadra reguladores como inimigos do progresso, todo custo de conformidade vira uma ameaça existencial e toda proposta de imposto vira um ataque ao futuro. A crença e o interesse próprio se reforçam até você não conseguir mais distinguir o que está no comando.

Tem também uma coisa mais antiga em jogo. O Thiel tem aquela frase que competição é para perdedores e o jogo de verdade é construir um monopólio. O Andreessen e o Horowitz passaram a carreira sendo os caras descolados que batiam o establishment. Agora eles são o establishment, e a única forma de continuar rebelde é inventar um novo establishment pra combater. O princípio da precaução, a galera de segurança de IA, os reguladores da UE — esses são os novos dragões. Você não vira herói sem um inimigo.

E acho que tem também uma camada de status. No Vale do Silício, ser chamado de reacionário ou fascista virou quase um distintivo agora. Sinaliza que você não foi capturado pelo consenso, que está pensando por si mesmo. Quanto mais o establishment da Bay Area se retrai, mais isso confirma pra eles que são os que estão vendo claro. É um loop de retroalimentação que não precisa mais de validação externa.

Então sim, a ideologia é real. Mas é uma ideologia que cresceu dentro de uma bolha de sucesso total, que é o tipo mais perigoso, porque nada nunca empurra com força suficiente pra fazer eles duvidarem.

996e93a67db20657.en:
Searching for personal accounts of what they're like. 

They're two very different animals. Horowitz is the people person. Painfully shy as a kid, still has trouble making eye contact with strangers. A Netscape colleague described him as having an awkward user interface but said his life as an outsider gave him real empathy — he could get people to work together. Bill Campbell, the legendary coach who mentored Jobs and Bezos, called him one of the sharpest business leaders he knows. His wife Felicia, back when they were dating in the eighties, described him as a very nice person who loved rap music and bartended for a living. One interviewer who spent real time with him called him one of the best people they've ever spoken to — generous, patient, with a killer wit. He personally teaches every new hire at a sixteen z for an hour about the culture, and he used to fine people ten bucks a minute for being late to meetings with founders.

Andreessen is the opposite temperament. At his own wedding, Horowitz toasted him as grouchy Marc who'd gone through his whole life without anyone understanding him — farm town, Silicon Valley, nobody got him. Then he met Laura and became happy Marc. Andreessen himself has said he was an unhappy, grumpy, irascible character before her. A close friend told the New Yorker that when Marc feels disrespected, he can cut you out of his life like a cancer. The two of them fight like cats and dogs and then forget about it. Horowitz has also noted that Marc is actually more sensitive than people realize — he'll get upset about Ben's body language mid-sentence.

There's one dinner anecdote from a progressive journalist that stuck with me. Andreessen was going off about how much he hated growing up in rural Wisconsin, and then said something like, I'm glad there's OxyContin and video games to keep those people quiet. The journalist couldn't even be sure of the exact words, but the contempt was unmistakable. That's the Andreessen most people never see — the one behind the manifesto.

So are they nice? Horowitz, by most accounts, genuinely is — or at least works hard at being the kind of person people want to work for, which he says is the whole job of a CEO. Andreessen is more of a force than a person. Smart beyond almost anyone, loyal to the few who earn it, and cold to everyone else.
996e93a67db20657.tr:
Estou procurando relatos pessoais sobre como eles são na vida real.

São dois bichos bem diferentes. Horowitz é o cara que se dá bem com as pessoas. Era dolorosamente tímido quando criança, ainda tem dificuldade de fazer contato visual com estranhos. Um colega do Netscape descreveu ele como tendo uma interface de usuário meio esquisita, mas disse que a vida dele como outsider deu a ele uma empatia real — ele conseguia fazer as pessoas trabalharem juntas. Bill Campbell, o lendário coach que mentorou Jobs e Bezos, chamou ele de um dos líderes de negócios mais afiados que ele conhece. A mulher dele, Felicia, quando estavam namorando nos anos oitenta, descreveu ele como uma pessoa muito legal que adorava rap e trabalhava como bartender. Um entrevistador que passou um tempo real com ele disse que é uma das melhores pessoas com quem já conversou — generoso, paciente, com um humor afiado. Ele mesmo dá uma aula de uma hora para todo novo contratado da a16z sobre a cultura da empresa, e antigamente multava as pessoas em dez dólares por minuto de atraso em reuniões com fundadores.

Andreessen é o oposto de temperamento. No próprio casamento dele, Horowitz brindou chamando ele de «o Marc rabugento» que passou a vida inteira sem que ninguém entendesse ele — cidadezinha do interior, Vale do Silício, ninguém sacava. Aí ele conheceu a Laura e virou o Marc feliz. O próprio Andreessen já disse que era um cara infeliz, rabugento e irritadiço antes dela. Um amigo próximo contou para a New Yorker que, quando o Marc se sente desrespeitado, ele te corta da vida dele como se fosse um câncer. Os dois brigam feito cão e gato e depois esquecem. Horowitz também já comentou que o Marc é na verdade mais sensível do que as pessoas imaginam — ele fica chateado com a linguagem corporal do Ben no meio de uma frase.

Tem uma história de um jantar que ficou na minha cabeça, contada por um jornalista progressista. Andreessen estava detonando o quanto odiava ter crescido no interior de Wisconsin, e aí falou algo tipo: «Ainda bem que existe OxyContin e videogame para manter essa gente quieta». O jornalista nem teve certeza das palavras exatas, mas o desprezo era inconfundível. É esse Andreessen que a maioria das pessoas nunca vê — o que está por trás do manifesto.

Então, eles são gente boa? Horowitz, pela maioria dos relatos, realmente é — ou pelo menos se esforça muito para ser o tipo de pessoa para quem as pessoas querem trabalhar, que ele diz ser o trabalho inteiro de um CEO. Andreessen é mais uma força da natureza do que uma pessoa. Inteligente como quase ninguém, leal com os poucos que conquistam isso, e frio com todo mundo mais.

0b09fd34ad4e01a7.en: So who are the people that Andreessen, is loyal to or considers his people?
0b09fd34ad4e01a7.tr: Então quem são as pessoas que o Andreessen considera leais ou considera «os dele»?

32c418933071e9b9.en:
The inner circle is small and pretty fixed. Laura is the core. He met her at a New Year's Eve dinner in two thousand five, they talked for six and a half hours, and he sent her seventeen emails the next day. He has called her and her father his replacement family — the people who finally understood him after a lifetime of not being understood. Her dad John Arrillaga, the Silicon Valley land baron, is basically a second father to him. They're both bald, both self-made, both magisterial, and Laura once showed a photo of the two side by side and said, quite two peas in a pod.

Ben Horowitz is the other permanent fixture. Thirty years of partnership, constant screaming matches, and neither has ever walked. Horowitz stayed at Netscape when forty percent of the company left, and that loyalty is what made Andreessen start trusting people at all.

Beyond that, it's thin. He has a soft spot for people from his Wisconsin roots — there's a story where colleagues called an internet pawnshop idea immoral, and Andreessen went off on them, saying if you've got no money and need to pawn your watch to feed your kids, that's not immoral, you rich motherfuckers. He knew that guy. He'd been that guy.

Everyone else is more like colleagues he respects for their output than people he cares about. Tim Ferriss said talking to him is like taking a final exam every time. David Senra said he's one of the smartest humans he's ever met but clearly studies up before every meeting. The loyalty runs one direction — he gives it to family and to the one partner who never flinched, and he expects the world to earn the rest.

The interesting question is whether that circle can ever grow. He's fifty-five now, and the pattern so far is that people get in early or they don't get in at all.

O círculo interno é pequeno e bem fixo. Laura é o núcleo. Ele conheceu ela num jantar de Ano Novo em 2005, eles conversaram seis horas e meia, e no dia seguinte ele mandou dezessete e-mails para ela. Ele já chamou ela e o pai dela de família substituta — as pessoas que finalmente entenderam ele depois de uma vida inteira sem ser entendido. O pai dela, John Arrillaga, o barão de terras do Vale do Silício, é basicamente um segundo pai para ele. Os dois são carecas, os dois se fizeram sozinhos, os dois têm um ar majestoso, e a Laura uma vez mostrou uma foto dos dois lado a lado e disse: são duas ervilhas na mesma vagem.

Ben Horowitz é o outro pilar permanente. Trinta anos de sociedade, brigas aos gritos o tempo todo, e nenhum dos dois nunca foi embora. Horowitz ficou no Netscape quando quarenta por cento da empresa saiu, e foi essa lealdade que fez o Andreessen começar a confiar nas pessoas.

Fora isso, é ralo. Ele tem um carinho especial por gente que veio da mesma raiz de Wisconsin — tem uma história em que os colegas chamaram uma ideia de casa de penhores na internet de imoral, e o Andreessen explodiu com eles, dizendo: se você não tem dinheiro e precisa penhorar o relógio para alimentar os filhos, isso não é imoral, seus filhos da puta ricos. Ele conhecia aquele cara. Ele já tinha sido aquele cara.

Todo mundo mais é mais tipo colegas que ele respeita pelo que produzem do que pessoas que ele realmente se importa. O Tim Ferriss disse que conversar com ele é como fazer uma prova final toda vez. David Senra disse que ele é um dos humanos mais inteligentes que já conheceu, mas que claramente estuda antes de cada reunião. A lealdade vai só num sentido — ele dá para a família e para o único sócio que nunca vacilou, e espera que o mundo conquiste o resto.

A pergunta interessante é se esse círculo pode algum dia crescer. Ele tem cinquenta e cinco anos agora, e o padrão até aqui é que as pessoas entram cedo ou não entram nunca.

0006f763e9922646.en: Where does Elon fit into this whole narrative?
0006f763e9922646.tr: Onde o Elon entra nessa história toda?

2b84decedc81e25a.en:
Let me check the current state of the Andreessen-Elon relationship. 

Elon is the one guy Andreessen treats almost like a peer. He's called him the only CEO who can sit down with engineers as a peer on rocket design, said working at one of his companies is like being dropped into a zone of shocking competence, and described his management style as going back to Henry Ford and Carnegie — the owner-operator industrialists. Andreessen has also said Musk and Trump are the only two people he's ever met who are completely transparent, saying the same thing in public and private.

Financially, a sixteen z is a SpaceX investor, and Musk's trust showed up on the shareholder list for X Holdings. When SpaceX absorbed xAI earlier this year, Andreessen and a writer at the firm published a piece framing it as the foundation for an AI-powered space economy — orbital data centers, solar-powered compute, the whole vision.

Politically they arrived at Trump from different directions. Musk jumped first, after the Twitter acquisition and the lawfare. Andreessen came later, after the Biden lunch. But once both were in, they overlapped hard — Andreessen spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago during the transition while Musk ran DOGE, and a sixteen z led funding for a startup called Special, built by former DOGE staffers including Musk's right-hand man Steve Davis.

The tension is that Andreessen is a VC who backs lots of companies, while Musk builds everything himself and doesn't really need outside capital. So the relationship is admiration plus capital, not quite mentorship. Andreessen studies Musk the way he studies every founder — but with more genuine awe than usual.

One wrinkle: back in twenty twenty-two, Andreessen tweeted that Elon must not be allowed to impose his refusal to censor on us, right after Musk bought Twitter. That was before the political convergence. Whether that old friction is fully gone or just buried under shared interests is the part nobody outside that circle actually knows.

599c058ea208de90.en: How did Musk become a Trump fanboy?
599c058ea208de90.tr: Como é que o Musk virou fã do Trump?

7780d9569bfcbced.en:
Checking how that shift unfolded. 

It was a slow burn that turned into a sprint. Musk voted for Biden in twenty twenty, called himself a moderate Democrat. The drift started with the Twitter buy in April twenty twenty-two. Taking over the platform put him face to face with content moderation fights, government pressure, and the left's fury at him personally. He reinstated Trump's account, called the ban morally bad, and by mid twenty twenty-two declared the Democrats the party of division and hate. Trump, for his part, had called Musk a name at a rally that same year, and Musk publicly told him to hang up his hat. So it wasn't love at first sight.

Twenty twenty-three, he backed DeSantis instead, even helped launch that campaign on X. But DeSantis flamed out, and Musk's grievances with Biden kept stacking — SEC lawsuits, NLRB cases, California's gender notification law that pushed SpaceX to Texas. By early twenty twenty-four he was privately meeting Trump at Mar-a-Lago and pitching other billionaires at a Palm Beach dinner, framing it around the border and election integrity, not ideology.

The public flip came July thirteenth, twenty twenty-four, about an hour after the Butler shooting. Musk endorsed within the hour, then went nuclear — roughly two hundred eighty-eight million dollars through America PAC, swing-state canvassing, a million-dollar-a-day giveaway, dark MAGA rallies. On Tucker Carlson he said if Trump loses, this is the last election, and joked about his prison sentence. That's not fandom. That's someone who believes losing means personal destruction.

The coda is the part people forget. They imploded in June twenty twenty-five over Trump's tax bill — Musk called it a disgusting abomination, claimed Trump was in the Epstein files, Trump threatened his contracts. Musk left DOGE in May twenty twenty-five, admitted on Isaacson's podcast he got carried away. Now in twenty twenty-six they're thawed again — Trump gave him the National Medal of Science, called him a national treasure, and Musk is dropping another two hundred seventy-six million on the midterms.

So the honest read: it was never really about Trump. It was about Musk's enemies, his businesses, and his conviction that a Democratic win meant jail. Trump was the available weapon. The Andreessen comparison is the mirror — same grievance stack, same self-preservation math, different personality. Andreessen intellectualizes it into a manifesto. Musk just buys the outcome.

One thing worth sitting with: Musk told Isaacson the only way to fix the deficit is AI and robots, not government. That's the through-line across everything he does now — politics as a means to protect the machine.
7780d9569bfcbced.tr:
Vou verificar como foi essa virada.

d5b3b055d0af9948.en: Can you, uh, rewind, rewind a second? What was this about the shooting?
d5b3b055d0af9948.tr: Pode, hum, voltar um segundo? O que foi isso do tiroteio?

149f4ea5395f63f9.en:
July thirteenth, twenty twenty-four, Butler, Pennsylvania. Trump was giving a speech at an outdoor rally when a twenty-year-old named Thomas Matthew Crooks fired from a rooftop about a hundred thirty yards away. One bullet grazed Trump's right ear, cutting it. Two people in the crowd died — a firefighter named Corey Comperatore who shielded his family, and an attendee named David Dutch. Two others were critically wounded. The Secret Service killed Crooks within seconds.

What made it politically explosive wasn't just the shooting. It was the image. Trump standing up, blood running down his face, pumping his fist and shouting "Fight, fight, fight" while the crowd chanted. That photo became the single most powerful visual of the entire campaign. Musk saw it and posted his endorsement about an hour later. He'd been hedging for months, but that moment removed whatever was left of his hesitation.

The Butler failure also triggered a massive Secret Service overhaul and became a permanent talking point — Musk later claimed it proved the government was either incompetent or complicit.
149f4ea5395f63f9.tr:

Uma bala raspou na orelha direita do Trump, cortando ela. Duas pessoas na plateia morreram — um bombeiro chamado Corey Comperatore que protegeu a família, e um participante chamado David Dutch. Outros dois ficaram gravemente feridos. O Serviço Secreto matou o Crooks em segundos.

O que tornou isso politicamente explosivo não foi só o tiroteio. Foi a imagem. Trump se levantando, sangue escorrendo no rosto, erguendo o punho e gritando «Fight, fight, fight» enquanto a multidão cantava. Aquela foto virou a imagem mais poderosa de toda a campanha. Musk viu e postou o endosso cerca de uma hora depois. Ele vinha hesitando há meses, mas aquele momento acabou com o que restava da hesitação dele.

O fracasso de Butler também disparou uma reforma gigantesca no Serviço Secreto e virou um ponto de discussão permanente — Musk depois alegou que provava que o governo era ou incompetente ou cúmplice.

c13e0a76e9d04e41.en:
All three, stacked in layers. The deepest layer is the civilizational one. Musk has spent years saying birth rates are collapsing, AI could end humanity, and the West is losing its edge. He genuinely believes the administrative state is the bottleneck — that every regulation, every lawsuit, every compliance department is a tax on the future. In his head, Trump isn't the crazy option. Trump is the only option willing to break the machine. That's the frame he uses with people like Carlson: if this election is lost, democracy itself is over, because the other side won't allow another fair one.

But underneath that is something more personal and less noble. The Tucker interview is the tell. He laughed about it, but he asked how long his prison sentence would be, whether he'd see his children. That's not a man thinking about humanity. That's a man who thinks the other side will come for him. The SEC cases, the NLRB rulings, the Twitter Files, the sense that the entire apparatus of government had turned against him — it stopped being about policy and became about survival. He told Carlson he'd been trashing Kamala nonstop because he believed a Harris win meant X gets dismantled and he gets prosecuted.

And then there's the pure spite layer, which he barely hides. He bought Twitter partly out of grievance. He moved SpaceX to Texas out of spite for one California law. When Trump pulled the EV mandate, Musk went nuclear on Truth Social within hours. This is a guy who keeps score and doesn't forgive.

The interesting part is what he's saying now. On Isaacson's podcast just this week, he admitted he kinda got carried away with DOGE, that he should have stayed in the background for a month or two instead of four. He's saying the only way to fix the deficit is AI and robots, not government cuts — which is basically him walking back the whole project. So even his own certainty is wobbling. The savior narrative and the spite narrative are still running, but the man in the middle is starting to notice they don't quite add up.

Ele realmente acredita que o Estado administrativo é o gargalo — que toda regulação, todo processo, todo departamento de conformidade é um imposto sobre o futuro. Na cabeça dele, Trump não é a opção maluca. Trump é a única opção disposta a quebrar a máquina. É esse o enquadramento que ele usa com gente como o Carlson: se perdermos essa eleição, a própria democracia acabou, porque o outro lado não vai permitir outra eleição justa.

Mas por baixo disso tem algo mais pessoal e menos nobre. A entrevista no Tucker é o sinal. Ele riu, mas perguntou quanto tempo seria a pena de prisão dele, se ainda veria os filhos. Isso não é um homem pensando na humanidade. É um homem que acha que o outro lado vai atrás dele. Os casos da SEC, as decisões do NLRB, os Twitter Files, a sensação de que todo o aparato do governo tinha se voltado contra ele — deixou de ser sobre política e virou sobrevivência. b250ddbff8375fd3.en: How, how does Elon view the, uh, USAID cuts? What's up with that?
b250ddbff8375fd3.tr: Como o Elon vê os cortes na USAID? O que rolou com isso?

5c6b2b6f6e01e84d.en:
Searching for Musk's latest on USAID. 

Musk's view is that USAID was a criminal organization that needed to die. On February third, twenty twenty-five, he posted that he'd spent the weekend feeding it into the wood chipper and could have gone to great parties instead. He framed it as the purest example of waste — taxpayer money going to corrupt politicians, militants, and DEI programs abroad instead of Americans.

The scale was brutal. USAID's workforce went from about thirteen thousand six hundred to two hundred forty-one — a ninety-eight percent cut. Nearly seven thousand of its seventy-five hundred awards got terminated, worth about seventy-nine billion dollars in obligations. Rubio later said five thousand two hundred of six thousand two hundred programs were eliminated, with the surviving eighteen percent folded into the State Department. DOGE claimed twenty-eight point three billion in savings from USAID alone.

Musk's defense is that zero people died because of it. He called reports of child deaths nonsense, and when Congressman Ro Khanna cited a Lancet study estimating fourteen million deaths by twenty thirty, Musk threatened to sue him. He did admit to accidentally cutting Ebola detection and response programs in the DRC, which experts say hurt the outbreak response there. An independent tracker put excess deaths above seven hundred eighty thousand in the first year, over half a million of them children. A federal judge in March twenty twenty-five ruled the cuts likely unconstitutional and blocked further action, though the administration appealed.

The part that cuts against the pure-ideologue story is what Musk says now. On Isaacson's podcast this week he admitted he got carried away, that he should have stayed in the background for a month or two instead of four months. He's also saying the deficit can't be fixed by cutting government — only AI and robots will do it. So even he seems to have concluded the wood chipper didn't solve the problem he thought it would.

One angle worth sitting with: USAID was also one of the last remaining soft-power instruments the US had for shaping the developing world. Rubio himself said pulling it into State had a direct impact on regional stability. Whether that's a feature or a bug depends entirely on whether you think American influence abroad was worth having in the first place.
5c6b2b6f6e01e84d.tr:
Estou a procurar as declarações mais recentes do Musk sobre a USAID.

A visão do Musk é que a USAID era uma organização criminosa que precisava morrer. A 3 de fevereiro de 2025, ele publicou que tinha passado o fim de semana a enfiá-la no triturador de madeira e que podia ter ido a festas incríveis em vez disso. Ele apresentou-a como o exemplo mais puro de desperdício — dinheiro dos contribuintes a ir para políticos corruptos, militantes e programas de DEI no estrangeiro em vez de ir para os americanos.

A escala foi brutal. O pessoal da USAID passou de cerca de 13.600 para 241 — um corte de 98%. Quase 7.000 dos 7.500 contratos foram terminados, no valor de cerca de 79 mil milhões de dólares em obrigações. O Rubio disse mais tarde que 5.200 de 6.200 programas foram eliminados, e os 18% que sobraram foram integrados no Departamento de Estado. O DOGE reivindicou 28,3 mil milhões de dólares em poupanças só da USAID.

A defesa do Musk é que zero pessoas morreram por causa disso. Ele chamou de nonsense os relatos de mortes de crianças, e quando o congressista Ro Khanna citou um estudo da Lancet que estimava 14 milhões de mortes até 2030, o Musk ameaçou processá-lo. Ele admitiu ter cortado acidentalmente os programas de deteção e resposta ao Ébola na RDC, o que os especialistas dizem que prejudicou a resposta ao surto lá. Um rastreador independente colocou as mortes em excesso acima de 780 mil no primeiro ano, mais de meio milhão delas crianças. Um juiz federal em março de 2025 decidiu que os cortes eram provavelmente inconstitucionais e bloqueou mais ações, embora a administração tenha recorrido.

A parte que desmonta a história do ideólogo puro é o que o Musk diz agora. No podcast do Isaacson esta semana ele admitiu que se deixou levar, que devia ter ficado em segundo plano durante um ou dois meses em vez de quatro. Também está a dizer que o défice não se resolve cortando governo — só a IA e os robôs vão conseguir. Por isso até ele parece ter concluído que o triturador não resolveu o problema que ele pensava que ia resolver.

O próprio Rubio disse que integrá-la no State teve um impacto direto na estabilidade regional. Se isso é uma funcionalidade ou um bug depende inteiramente de se achas que a influência americana no estrangeiro valia a pena ter em primeiro lugar.

His argument is structural. He says the aid pipeline was so broken by corruption and bureaucracy that the dollars never translated into lives saved in the first place, so you can't attribute deaths to removing a channel that wasn't delivering. He also points out that some money got rerouted through the UN and bilateral deals, and that the death estimates come from models that assume every dollar spent equals a life saved, which he calls fantasy math. The Lancet's fourteen million figure, for instance, assumes USAID's entire historical impact would vanish instantly and permanently.

The counter is that even if the system was wasteful, the PEPFAR disruption data is pretty direct — seventeen hundred sites closed, seventy-seven thousand fewer children on treatment. That's not a model, that's a count. But Musk's response to that is basically: show me the bodies, prove the counterfactual. And since you can't run the experiment twice, it stays a fight over whose inference you trust.

What's striking is he treats this like an engineering problem where the null hypothesis is no harm, and the burden of proof sits entirely on the people saying people died.
ece87b87d49de966.tr:
O argumento dele é estrutural. Ele diz que o canal de ajuda estava tão corroído pela corrupção e pela burocracia que os dólares nunca se traduziam em vidas salvas para começar, por isso não se podem atribuir mortes a remover um canal que não estava a entregar nada. Ele também aponta que parte do dinheiro foi redirecionada através da ONU e de acordos bilaterais, e que as estimativas de mortes vêm de modelos que assumem que cada dólar gasto equivale a uma vida salva, o que ele chama de matemática de fantasia. O número de 14 milhões da Lancet, por exemplo, assume que todo o impacto histórico da USAID desapareceria instantânea e permanentemente.

A contra-argumentação é que, mesmo que o sistema fosse desperdício, os dados da disrupção do PEPFAR são bastante diretos — 1.700 centros fechados, 77 mil crianças a menos em tratamento. Isso não é um modelo, é uma contagem. Mas a resposta do Musk a isso é basicamente: mostrem-me os corpos, provem o contrafactual. E como não se pode correr o experimento duas vezes, fica uma luta sobre em quem confiar na inferência.

O que é impressionante é que ele trata isto como um problema de engenharia em que a hipótese nula é não haver mal nenhum, e o ónus da prova fica inteiramente nas pessoas que dizem que morreram pessoas.

Digging into the actual corruption numbers. 

The ninety percent figure doesn't come from corruption audits. It comes from a USAID localization report showing that about twelve percent of funding went directly to local organizations in developing countries. The other eighty-eight percent flowed through American contractors, international NGOs, and in-kind goods — HIV drugs, food, bed nets. That's not theft. That's how the delivery system works. Musk amplified a quote from a guy named Walter Kerr at a group called Unlock Aid, who said less than ten percent reaches communities — but Kerr was talking about the same localization stat, not about money vanishing.

The actual audit numbers are starkly different. SIGAR, the Special Inspector General for Afghan Reconstruction, ran two hundred eighty-four financial audits covering ten billion dollars in spending across the toughest war zone on earth. Only zero point three percent was disallowed — about thirty-one million dollars. In Ukraine, audits of nearly five hundred million found just under two hundred thousand in questioned costs, and five of twelve implementers had zero findings. USAID's own inspector general audited forty-nine billion in one six-month stretch and flagged about eight and a half million in questioned costs.

There were real fraud cases — a five-hundred-fifty-million-dollar bribery scheme involving a USAID contracting officer, nine million diverted to an al-Qaeda affiliate in Syria, payroll fraud in Mali. But those are individual prosecutions, not a systemic ninety percent loss. The former USAID inspector general, Paul Martin, said DOGE never once referenced actual IG criminal allegations. And when the White House put out a list of twelve waste examples, fact-checkers found eleven misleading or flat wrong — three of the four headline items weren't even USAID-funded.

So the honest read is: overhead and contractor margins are a legitimate gripe, maybe thirty to sixty percent on some programs per one academic estimate. But ninety percent siphoned off? The audit trail doesn't support it.

Searching for Sacks' political evolution. 

Sacks was never really a liberal. He was a libertarian conservative from day one. At Stanford in the early nineties he co-wrote The Diversity Myth with Thiel, a book attacking multiculturalism and political correctness on campus. He gave to McCain and Romney, then in twenty sixteen donated to Hillary and the DNC — which looks like an outlier but was more about staying in the Valley's social good graces than conviction. He sat out twenty twenty entirely.

The real turn came with COVID. San Francisco's lockdowns radicalized him. He moved to Florida for a stretch, praised DeSantis, and started funding recall campaigns against SF school board members, DA Chesa Boudin, and LA DA George Gascón. On the All-In podcast he called January sixth an insurrection and said Trump was disqualified — then spent the next two years walking that back. By twenty twenty-two he was dropping a million dollars on a JD Vance super PAC. In June twenty twenty-four he hosted a twelve-million-dollar Trump fundraiser at his Pacific Heights mansion, tickets five hundred grand a couple, and endorsed the same day. He framed it as breaking the ice so other tech billionaires could come out.

The Anthropic fight is where it gets personal and structural at once. Sacks' core thesis is that safety rhetoric is regulatory capture dressed up as altruism. His September post is the manifesto: Dario and Sam have a duopoly on frontier intelligence, so if they want to slow down, fine — but stop pretending they need antitrust waivers and government approval to do it. Call it a cartel. He also went after METR, the safety evaluator Anthropic funds, as not independent. Then there's the June Fable incident — a trusted partner reportedly jailbroke Anthropic's Mythos guardrails, the admin asked Dario to fix it or pull the model, he refused, and Sacks says that's what triggered the export controls. Anthropic disputes the framing.

Underneath all of it sits the business angle. Craft Ventures has stakes in crypto and AI companies that benefit from loose rules. Sacks sold his personal holdings in Meta, Amazon, TSMC, and xAI when he took the czar job, but the firm's portfolio didn't vanish. 371c205541f1b170.en:
He launched the first one in twenty seventeen with Ian Osborne's Hedosophia, ticker IPOA, six hundred million raised. Virgin Galactic merged in October twenty nineteen and the stock ripped — that one deal made him the SPAC King overnight. He reserved tickers IPOA all the way through IPOZ, signaling he planned twenty-six of these things. In twenty twenty he doubled up with IPOB and IPOC, three hundred sixty and seven hundred twenty million. Then came Opendoor, Clover Health, SoFi — each with a one-page investment memo he tweeted like a product launch. At the peak in early twenty twenty-one he was filing for seven more, IPOG through IPOZ, before the market turned.

The outcomes were brutal for public holders. Virgin Galactic is down about ninety-eight percent from its peak and halted commercial flights indefinitely. Opendoor down roughly ninety-five from its high. Clover down around ninety. Akili Interactive, a digital-therapeutics company, got acquired at forty-three cents a share. ProKidney down about ninety-five. SoFi is the only one that ever printed a positive return, and even that sat below trust value for years. Bloomberg's median across his completed deals is about a seventy-five percent loss. Senator Warren's investigation found SPAC sponsors averaged nine hundred fifty-eight percent returns from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-one while the companies they took public consistently underperformed.

The kicker is what Chamath did personally. He sold most of his Virgin Galactic stake in March twenty twenty-one for around two hundred million, and by the NYT's reporting in December twenty twenty-two he'd roughly doubled the seven hundred fifty million he'd put in across his SPACs — by exiting early while retail investors who followed his tweets were left holding the bag. Hindenburg also flagged that he hadn't disclosed an active Medicare fraud investigation at Clover when he was promoting it; the company later settled shareholder suits for twenty-two million.

He's since admitted the structural problem himself — in a twenty twenty-six interview he said his incentives were totally and fundamentally misaligned because he could do a deal and still get paid, called it a blemish on his record. And in October twenty twenty-five he launched a new SPAC but publicly told retail investors to stay away, saying the vehicles aren't ideal for most of them — ninety-eight point seven percent of it went to hand-picked institutions first.

The pattern that ties it to everything else we've discussed: he built a machine where the sponsor wins whether or not the investor does, then spent two years telling a mass audience it was the opposite. That's not a market failure. That's a pitch.

One angle worth pulling on — the same misalignment shows up in how he talks about politics now. Access and attention as the real currency, outcomes secondary. Want me to trace whether that SPAC-era logic is what he's running on the All-In mic?
371c205541f1b170.tr:
Ele lançou o primeiro em 2017 com a Hedosophia do Ian Osborne, ticker IPOA, seiscentos milhões captados. Ele reservou os tickers de IPOA até IPOZ, sinalizando que planejava fazer vinte e seis dessas coisas. Em 2020 ele dobrou a aposta com IPOB e IPOC, trezentos e sessenta e setecentos e vinte milhões. Depois vieram Opendoor, Clover Health, SoFi — cada uma com um memo de investimento de uma página que ele tweetava como se fosse lançamento de produto. No pico, no começo de 2021, ele estava registrando mais sete, de IPOG até IPOZ, antes de o mercado virar.

Os resultados foram brutais pros investidores de varejo. A Virgin Galactic está uns noventa e oito por cento abaixo do pico e parou os voos comerciais por tempo indeterminado. Opendoor caiu mais ou menos noventa e cinco do topo. Clover em torno de noventa. A Akili Interactive, uma empresa de terapias digitais, foi comprada por quarenta e três centavos a ação. ProKidney caiu uns noventa e cinco. SoFi é a única que deu retorno positivo, e mesmo assim ficou abaixo do valor do trust por anos. A investigação da senadora Warren descobriu que os sponsors de SPAC tiveram em média novecentos e cinquenta e oito por cento de retorno de 2019 a 2021, enquanto as empresas que eles levaram a público consistentemente tiveram desempenho ruim.

O que pesa mesmo é o que o Chamath fez pessoalmente. Ele vendeu a maior parte da posição na Virgin Galactic em março de 2021 por uns duzentos milhões, e segundo a reportagem do NYT em dezembro de 2022 ele tinha mais ou menos dobrado os setecentos e cinquenta milhões que colocou nos SPACs — saindo cedo enquanto os investidores de varejo que seguiam os tweets dele ficaram segurando o prejuízo. O padrão que liga isso a tudo que a gente discutiu: ele montou uma máquina em que o sponsor ganha independentemente de o investidor ganhar, e depois passou dois anos dizendo pra uma audiência enorme que era o contrário. Isso não é falha de mercado. É um pitch.

Um ângulo que vale explorar — o mesmo desalinhamento aparece no jeito como ele fala de política agora. Acesso e atenção como a moeda de verdade, resultados em segundo plano. Quer que eu trace se essa lógica da era SPAC é o que ele está rodando no microfone do All-In?

aa07097b09c7c83a.en:
Searching for how Chamath and Sacks interact. 

They're the closest pair in the group. Chamath texted Jason Calacanis during COVID to start the pod, Sacks joined for episode two, and the four of them have been inseparable ever since — four hundred thirty-five episodes, a group chat, an annual summit. On the show Chamath is the Dictator, the finance guy who goes on semi-scholarly digressions while the others listen. Sacks is Rainman, the politics and macro brain who barely emotes. Slate noted the dynamic is affectionate but real — they squabble over inflation numbers, Chamath and Jason went at it over VC culpability in FTX, and one fusion debate got so heated Jason wondered if the friendship was on the rocks.

The political pivot happened together. After January sixth Chamath called Trump a piece-of-shit scumbag and Sacks said he'd disqualified himself. Two years later they co-hosted that twelve-million-dollar fundraiser at Sacks's Broadcliff estate in Pacific Heights — tickets fifty grand, host committee half a million a couple. Sacks credited JD Vance with making it happen; both backed Vance for VP. When the NYT ran its piece on Sacks profiting from the czar role, Chamath posted that even the hit piece's authors admitted Sacks was doing a good job. When Chamath turned fifty in September, Trump sent him a personal birthday letter after his son Braden interned at the White House — Sacks called it impressive, noting it takes time out of the president's schedule.

The one structural difference: Sacks is now inside the administration with actual power, while Chamath is the outside amplifier with the audience. Vanity Fair's read is that All-In became a direct line to the White House — one attendee put it that way flat out. So the dynamic is less two equals and more a broadcaster and his most powerful listener, which is a different kind of friendship than it used to be.

The thing I find interesting is that Chamath's whole brand is contrarian — he'll fight anyone on the pod. But on Sacks he's never once pushed back publicly, even when the NYT story was the juiciest possible target. That's either loyalty or self-interest, and with Chamath it's hard to fully separate the two.

No programa o Chamath é o Ditador, o cara de finanças que faz digressões meio acadêmicas enquanto os outros escutam. O Sacks é o Rainman, o cérebro de política e macro que quase não demonstra emoção. O Slate notou que a dinâmica é carinhosa mas real — eles brigam por números de inflação, o Chamath e o Jason se pegaram feio sobre a culpa do VC no FTX, e um debate sobre fusão esquentou tanto que o Jason chegou a achar que a amizade estava por um fio.

Dois anos depois eles co-organizaram aquela festa de doze milhões de dólares na casa do Sacks em Broadcliff, em Pacific Heights — ingresso a cinquenta mil, comitê de anfitriões meio milhão por casal. A única diferença estrutural: o Sacks agora está dentro da administração com poder de verdade, enquanto o Chamath é o amplificador externo com a audiência. Mas com o Sacks ele nunca deu um contraponto público, nem quando a matéria do NYT era o alvo mais suculento possível. Isso é lealdade ou interesse próprio, e com o Chamath é difícil separar completamente os dois.

61890c55b3fa75c7.en:
Jason's the operator of the four. 

Brooklyn-born, Greek and Armenian parents, grew up working class in a rough neighborhood. Syracuse for undergrad, then straight into Silicon Alley in the nineties — he ran a web design shop, did early AOL work, and was one of those guys who was physically present for the whole dot-com boom and bust in New York. That's the key difference from the other three: Chamath, Sacks, and Andreessen all had elite pedigrees and rode one rocket. Jason lived through the crash, rebuilt, crashed again with Mahalo in twenty fourteen when Google's Panda update gutted his traffic overnight. He's the only one of the four who's been broke more than once and talks about it openly.

His real skill is media and distribution, not investing. This Week in Startups has been running since two thousand nine — over fourteen hundred episodes. LAUNCH became the thing: a festival and accelerator that turned into a ten-million-dollar fund where he invests in a hundred startups a year. He's the third or fourth investor in Uber, which is the credential he leans on hardest. After Musk bought Twitter he helped run the company alongside Sacks for a stretch. Sacks is also a limited partner in his fund, which is the financial thread tying them together.

Politically he's the one who insists he's always been a moderate independent — voted Republican maybe one in three times, he says, living in New York, LA, and SF where there wasn't much choice. The shift wasn't ideological so much as personal. Elon and Sacks are close friends, they went into the administration, and Jason's framing is basically: if Trump is going to surround himself with the smartest entrepreneurs I know instead of Bannon types, I'm in. He doesn't love the style, doesn't care about the cruelty, cares about less government and the founder class.

What's interesting right now is he's started drifting again. Two days ago he posted a five-point America-first list telling Trump to raise the minimum wage to fifteen, end the Iran war, fund trade schools, mandate starter homes, and donate half the family's gains to Invest America accounts. He's also saying the midterms look like a purple tide, not a red one, and that MAGA feels double-crossed. So he's not a true believer like Sacks — he's a guy whose loyalty tracks proximity to power and whose principles flex when the room changes. The Bulwark ran him in June basically making that exact point: tech oligarchs would be fine with an oligarchy if it kept taxes low.

The contrast with the others is that Jason has no fortress. No fund with billions, no White House title, no manifesto. He's a broadcaster with an audience and a thin portfolio, which means his politics are the most reactive of the four — and the most likely to flip again if the winds change.

O Jason é o operador dos quatro.

Ele foi o terceiro ou quarto investidor do Uber, que é o credencial que ele mais usa. Depois que o Musk comprou o Twitter ele ajudou a tocar a empresa junto com o Sacks por um tempo. Elon e Sacks são amigos próximos, entraram na administração, e o enquadramento do Jason é basicamente: se o Trump vai se cercar dos empreendedores mais inteligentes que eu conheço em vez de gente tipo Bannon, eu topo. O Bulwark colocou ele em junho basicamente fazendo exatamente esse ponto: os oligarcas de tech ficariam bem com uma oligarquia se mantivesse os impostos baixos.

Ele é um locutor com audiência e um portfólio fino, o que significa que a política dele é a mais reativa dos quatro — e a mais propensa a virar de novo se o vento mudar.

5376b607e25ac5a8.en: Tell me a little bit about him. How did he become who he is?
5376b607e25ac5a8.tr: Me conta um pouco sobre ele. Como ele se tornou quem ele é?

aae309f19f76c88e.en:
Jason grew up in Brooklyn's Park Slope, the son of a Greek immigrant father who worked construction and an Armenian mother. He was the kid selling candy on the subway, doing odd jobs, scrappy by necessity. Syracuse gave him a degree but no money and no connections, so he moved back to New York and started a web design company in the early nineties when the internet was still a novelty. That's where he met the people building Silicon Alley — the pre-bubble New York tech scene that felt like a club of misfits compared to the Stanford-PayPal axis out west.

He got into AOL's greenhouse program, which was basically a farm team for early internet companies, and that gave him his first taste of institutional Silicon Valley. But he was always the outsider — the New Yorker, the non-engineer, the guy who understood distribution and hype better than code. That became his whole identity. He couldn't out-engineer Chamath or out-think Sacks, so he out-networked and out-marketed everyone.

Mahalo in two thousand seven was his big swing — a human-powered search engine meant to compete with Google. It burned through forty million dollars and collapsed when Google's algorithm changes killed his traffic. That's the moment that shaped him most. He went from being a guy who talked about winning to being a guy who had to explain losing on camera, every week, on his own podcast. And instead of disappearing, he turned that into the brand — the transparent founder who fails publicly and keeps going.

The LAUNCH festival in two thousand nine was the rebirth. He turned a conference into a media property into a fund, and the flywheel worked because he understood something the other three didn't: attention is the product. Uber's early investment gave him the story, but it was the relentless podcasting and event-running that built the audience. He's not a venture capitalist who happens to have a podcast. He's a media guy who happens to invest.

The political arc follows the same pattern. He was a Democrat-leaning New Yorker for most of his life, voted for Obama, gave to Democrats. The shift to Trump wasn't about ideology — it was about who was picking up the phone. Sacks and Musk were his friends, they were going into the administration, and Jason's entire career has been about being in the room. When the room moved right, he moved with it, and he rationalized it the way he rationalizes everything: as the pragmatic founder's choice.

What makes him different from the others is that he has no ideological armor. Chamath has access, Sacks has conviction, Andreessen has the manifesto. Jason has proximity and a microphone, and when proximity shifts, so does he. That's not weakness exactly — it's just honesty about what drives him, which the others dress up in philosophy.
aae309f19f76c88e.tr:
O Jason cresceu no Park Slope, no Brooklyn, filho de um pai imigrante grego que trabalhava na construção e de uma mãe armênia. Era o miúdo que vendia doces no metro, fazia biscates, um miúdo lutador por necessidade. Syracuse deu-lhe o diploma, mas nem dinheiro nem contactos, por isso voltou para Nova Iorque e montou uma empresa de design web no início dos anos noventa, quando a internet ainda era uma novidade. Foi aí que conheceu as pessoas que estavam a construir a Silicon Alley — a cena tech de Nova Iorque pré-bolha que parecia um clube de malucos comparada com o eixo Stanford-PayPal do outro lado do país.

Entrou no programa greenhouse da AOL, que era basicamente uma equipa de formação para as primeiras empresas de internet, e isso deu-lhe o primeiro contacto com o Silicon Valley institucional. Mas ele foi sempre o outsider — o nova-iorquino, o não engenheiro, o tipo que percebia de distribuição e de hype muito melhor do que de código. Isso tornou-se a sua identidade completa. Não conseguia superar o Chamath em engenharia nem o Sacks em pensamento, por isso superou toda a gente em networking e em marketing.

O Mahalo em 2007 foi a grande aposta dele — um motor de busca feito por humanos para competir com o Google. Queimou quarenta milhões de dólares e implodiu quando as alterações de algoritmo do Google mataram o tráfego dele. Esse foi o momento que mais o marcou. Passou de ser o tipo que falava em vencer para ser o tipo que tinha de explicar a derrota em frente às câmaras, todas as semanas, no próprio podcast. E em vez de desaparecer, transformou isso na marca — o fundador transparente que falha em público e continua.

O festival LAUNCH em 2009 foi o renascimento. Transformou uma conferência numa propriedade de media e depois num fundo, e o flywheel funcionou porque ele percebia uma coisa que os outros três não percebiam: a atenção é o produto. O investimento inicial na Uber deu-lhe a história, mas foi o podcasting implacável e a organização de eventos que construíram a audiência. Ele não é um venture capitalist que por acaso tem um podcast. É um gajo de media que por acaso investe.

O arco político segue o mesmo padrão. Foi um nova-iorquino com inclinação democrata a maior parte da vida, votou em Obama, doou aos democratas. A viragem para o Trump não foi por ideologia — foi por quem atendia o telefone. O Sacks e o Musk eram amigos dele, estavam a entrar na administração, e a carreira inteira do Jason tem sido sobre estar na sala. Quando a sala se mudou para a direita, ele mudou com ela, e racionalizou isso da mesma forma que racionaliza tudo: como a escolha pragmática de um founder.

O que o torna diferente dos outros é que não tem armadura ideológica. O Chamath tem acesso, o Sacks tem convicção, o Andreessen tem o manifesto. O Jason tem proximidade e um microfone, e quando a proximidade muda, ele muda também. Isso não é fraqueza exatamente — é só honestidade sobre o que realmente o move, coisa que os outros disfarçam de filosofia.

0bff365879cc6aac.en: What's known about his personality? What's he like?
0bff365879cc6aac.tr: O que se sabe sobre a personalidade dele? Como é que ele é?

540c0baa8a706367.en: Loud, fast, high-energy, always talking, always pitching. People who've worked with him describe him as relentless — the kind of guy who texts at midnight about a deal and expects a reply. He's openly emotional, cries on podcasts, talks about his failures with a kind of performative vulnerability that some find charming and others find exhausting. He name-drops constantly, not out of insecurity exactly but because proximity is his currency and he never lets you forget whose orbit you're in. He's also thin-skinned in a specific way — he'll take a punch about his investing record but bristles when anyone questions his sincerity or his work ethic. The Mahalo collapse taught him to own failure loudly, which is genuinely rare in this world, but it also taught him that confession can be a strategy. Whether the openness is armor or the real thing is something even his closest friends probably can't fully answer.
540c0baa8a706367.tr: Alto, rápido, cheio de energia, sempre a falar, sempre a fazer pitch. As pessoas que trabalharam com ele descrevem-no como implacável — o tipo de gajo que te manda mensagens à meia-noite sobre um negócio e espera resposta. É abertamente emocional, chora nos podcasts, fala das falhas com uma vulnerabilidade performativa que uns acham charmosa e outros acham exaustiva. Faz name-dropping constantemente, não exatamente por insegurança, mas porque a proximidade é a moeda dele e nunca te deixa esquecer em que órbita estás. Também é sensível de uma forma específica — aguenta piadas sobre o registo de investimentos, mas fica todo eriçado quando alguém questiona a sinceridade ou a ética de trabalho dele. O colapso do Mahalo ensinou-o a assumir o fracasso em voz alta, o que é genuinamente raro neste mundo, mas também lhe ensinou que a confissão pode ser uma estratégia. Se essa abertura é armadura ou é mesmo real, é algo que nem os amigos mais próximos dele conseguem responder por completo.

2758ff47c2bcabf1.en: What would he think if he read this conversation?
2758ff47c2bcabf1.tr: O que é que ele acharia se lesse esta conversa?

4c85e74512bc6ad9.en: He'd probably start by defending the Mahalo story — point out that he turned a forty-million-dollar loss into a fourteen-hundred-episode podcast and a media brand, which is more than most founders manage. Then he'd probably get to the part where I called him the most reactive of the four and bristle — not because it's wrong, but because he'd want to argue he was right about the founder class all along and the room just caught up. He'd skip past the Bulwark critique entirely or call it hit piece energy. The thing he'd actually sit with, maybe not say out loud, is the line about confession being a strategy. He's built his whole public persona on radical transparency, and hearing someone frame that as armor would land somewhere he doesn't have a ready answer for.
4c85e74512bc6ad9.tr: Provavelmente começava por defender a história do Mahalo — ia dizer que transformou uma perda de quarenta milhões de dólares num podcast de mil e quatrocentos episódios e numa marca de media, o que é mais do que a maioria dos founders consegue. Depois provavelmente chegava à parte em que eu o chamei o mais reativo dos quatro e ficava todo eriçado — não porque esteja errado, mas porque ia querer argumentar que sempre teve razão sobre a classe dos founders e que a sala é que acabou por lhe dar razão. Checking recent interviews for how he's doing now. 

The most recent window is the Katie Miller interview from October eleventh. He told her that when Groq sold to Nvidia for twenty billion, the internet was celebrating and he felt super down. He said to his wife Nat, I think I'm depressed. She asked why. He didn't know — he just kept thinking about everything that didn't go right. His own read on the pattern: he's felt the happiest before something great happened — before the Facebook IPO, before the Warriors championship, before the Slack IPO — and worse afterward. The anticipation is the peak. The arrival is a letdown.

On his fiftieth birthday in September he wrote a letter to his kids that he published publicly. He called the first fifty years an incredible adventure, acknowledged the deaths, the divorce, the financial pain, the mistakes — and told them not to dwell, just move on. What he listed as what's actually in your control: be kind, have fun, work on something meaningful, find your tribe, find perspective, find an incredible partner, have a bunch of kids, live an adventure, forgive your parents. Notably, zero mention of accomplishments or money. He wrote that it doesn't matter and won't matter, you'll be dust in under a hundred years.

On Lex Fridman last November he was even more direct. He said he's tried a hundred things on the happiness table and then two hundred more, and happiness isn't there. Money doesn't buy it — it just buys comfort that lets you amplify whatever happiness you already have. He also opened up about growing up with physical and psychological abuse, being hypervigilant his whole life, and how losing his best friend and his father within six months of each other broke the compartmentalization he'd used for thirty-five years. He's since forgiven his parents — says they did the best they could.

So the picture is: not miserable, not at peace either. He's in a strange middle where the external scoreboard keeps moving and the internal one never quite registers. The Groq moment is the cleanest data point — twenty billion dollars, and the feeling was deflation, not triumph.

Chamou aos primeiros cinquenta anos uma aventura incrível, reconheceu as mortes, o divórcio, a dor financeira, os erros — e disse-lhes para não ficarem presos nisso, só seguir em frente. f0bd240242e2675c.en:
Searching for fresh material on Thiel. 

Thiel is the deepest of the four. Born in Frankfurt in sixty-seven, moved to Cleveland at one, then to South West Africa where his dad ran a uranium mine near Swakopmund. He went to a German school there that used corporal punishment — striking kids' hands with a ruler — and he says that instilled a lifelong aversion to regimentation. Classmates called him a strange, strange boy. Chess prodigy, valedictorian at San Mateo High, then Stanford for philosophy. At Stanford he co-founded the Stanford Review with Sacks in eighty-seven, met René Girard whose mimetic theory became something like his intellectual religion, and co-wrote The Diversity Myth attacking campus multiculturalism. One Black student recalled him telling her South Africa's denial of civil rights was economically sound and moral issues were irrelevant. He didn't drink, didn't date, didn't crack jokes. A New Yorker writer who spent real time with him said he opens himself to all questions but his reasoning is so uninflected it becomes a barrier against intimacy. Musk said he's unconstrained by convention — almost everyone thinks by analogy or follows the crowd, Peter doesn't. Someone else who's known him over a decade said he's very cerebral and isn't sure how much value he places on intimate human emotions. He's never seen him express them.

The career is the legend. Confinity with Max Levchin in ninety-eight, merged with Musk's X.com into PayPal, sold to eBay for one point five billion in two thousand two. Then Palantir in two thousand three with Alex Karp, Founders Fund in two thousand five, and the five hundred thousand dollar check that bought him ten percent of Facebook in two thousand four. He's called the Don of the PayPal Mafia. His actual quote that matters most: "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." He wrote that in two thousand nine.

On Trump, he's been the most volatile of the group. First major tech figure to back him in twenty sixteen — one point two five million, RNC speech. Sat out twenty twenty entirely. Came back through Vance — fifteen million into his Senate super PAC, introduced them at Mar-a-Lago, privately urged Trump to pick him. Now in the second term he's openly critical. In September he told Mathias Döpfner the administration overcorrected with loyalty tests and staffed itself with people who are not very smart but very loyal. And just this month, Politico obtained audio from a private Nashville lecture where he said about the Iran war, I'm skeptical, I think we should not have done it, there were a lot of mistakes. He also said he doesn't think Trump is the Antichrist but worries if we get it wrong he could be the last katechon — a theological bulwark delaying evil. He's been giving a lecture series on the Antichrist. He's worth thirty-seven billion, lives in Buenos Aires, just bought the one hundred thirty million dollar Bel Air mansion called Casa Encantada, and Palantir is now sitting on one point four billion euros of European contracts while facing pushback in the UK over the NHS.

The through-line with the others: Sacks got the contrarian posture from him at Stanford. Andreessen got the accelerationism. Musk got the first-principles habit. Chamath got the access game. Thiel is the source code, and unlike the others he never needed the administration's validation — he was building toward something before Trump existed as a vehicle.

One thing worth sitting with: the Gawker takedown. He spent ten million secretly funding Hulk Hogan's lawsuit specifically to destroy a media company that had outed him. That's not ideology. That's a man who decided a grudge was worth a decade of lawfare and won.
f0bd240242e2675c.tr:
Estou a procurar material fresco sobre o Thiel.

O Thiel é o mais profundo dos quatro. Nascido em Frankfurt em 67, mudou-se para Cleveland com um ano, depois para o Sudoeste Africano, onde o pai geria uma mina de urânio perto de Swakopmund. Foi para uma escola alemã que usava castigos corporais — batia nas mãos das crianças com uma régua — e ele diz que isso lhe criou uma aversão para toda a vida à regimentação. Os colegas chamavam-no de «um rapaz estranho, muito estranho». Prodígio do xadrez, orador da turma no liceu de San Mateo, depois Universidade de Stanford em filosofia. Em Stanford co-fundou o Stanford Review com o Sacks em 87, conheceu o René Girard, cuja teoria mimética se tornou uma espécie de religião intelectual para ele, e co-escreveu The Diversity Myth, um ataque ao multiculturalismo no campus. Um estudante negro recorda-se dele a dizer-lhe que a negação dos direitos civis na África do Sul era economicamente sensata e que as questões morais eram irrelevantes. Não bebia, não namorava, não contava piadas. Um jornalista da New Yorker que passou bastante tempo com ele disse que o Thiel abre-se a todas as perguntas, mas o raciocínio dele é tão monocórdico que acaba por ser uma barreira contra a intimidade. O Musk disse que ele não é constrangido por convenções — quase toda a gente pensa por analogia ou segue a multidão, o Peter não. Alguém que o conhece há mais de uma década disse que ele é muito cerebral e não tem a certeza de quanto valor dá às emoções humanas íntimas. Nunca o viu expressá-las.

A carreira é lendária. Confinity com o Max Levchin em 98, fundiu-se com o X.com do Musk e virou PayPal, vendido ao eBay por mil e quinhentos milhões em 2002. Depois Palantir em 2003 com o Alex Karp, Founders Fund em 2005, e o cheque de quinhentos mil dólares que lhe deu dez por cento do Facebook em 2004. Chamam-lhe o Don da PayPal Mafia. A citação real dele que mais importa: «Já não acredito que a liberdade e a democracia sejam compatíveis.» Escreveu isso em 2009.

Sobre o Trump, tem sido o mais volátil do grupo. Foi a primeira grande figura da tecnologia a apoiá-lo em 2016 — um milhão e duzentos e cinquenta mil dólares, discurso na convenção republicana. Ficou de fora completamente em 2020. Voltou através do Vance — quinze milhões no super PAC dele para o Senado, apresentou-os em Mar-a-Lago, pressionou o Trump em privado para o escolher. Agora, no segundo mandato, é abertamente crítico. Em setembro disse ao Mathias Döpfner que a administração exagerou nos testes de lealdade e se rodeou de gente que não é muito inteligente mas é muito leal. E ainda este mês, o Politico obteve áudio de uma palestra privada em Nashville onde ele disse sobre a guerra no Irão: «Estou cético, acho que não devíamos ter feito isto, houve muitos erros.» Disse também que não acha que o Trump seja o Anticristo, mas que se errarmos ele pode ser o último katechon — um baluarte teológico que atrasa o mal. Tem dado uma série de palestras sobre o Anticristo. Vale trinta e sete mil milhões, vive em Buenos Aires, acabou de comprar a mansão de cento e trinta milhões de dólares em Bel Air chamada Casa Encantada, e a Palantir tem agora mil e quatrocentos milhões de euros em contratos europeus enquanto enfrenta resistência no Reino Unido por causa do NHS.

O fio condutor com os outros: o Sacks tirou dele a postura contrária na Stanford. O Andreessen tirou o aceleracionismo. O Musk tirou o hábito de pensar a partir de primeiros princípios. O Chamath tirou o jogo do acesso. O Thiel é o código-fonte, e ao contrário dos outros nunca precisou da validação da administração — já estava a construir algo antes de o Trump existir como veículo.

Uma coisa que vale a pena pensar: a destruição do Gawker. Gastou dez milhões a financiar em segredo a ação judicial do Hulk Hogan especificamente para destruir uma empresa de media que o tinha exposto. Isso não é ideologia. É um homem que decidiu que um rancor valia uma década de guerra judicial e ganhou.

Mimetic theory says desire isn't original — you want what others want, and that creates rivalry, scapegoating, and eventually violence that society resolves through ritual sacrifice. His friends and colleagues describe a man who's warm in private and opaque in public. Max Levchin, the other co-founder, stayed close and called him a genius who sees around corners but admitted he never fully understood what Thiel actually wanted for himself.

The open question with Thiel is whether he's playing a long game nobody else can see, or whether the contrarianism has become the identity and the ideas are just the costume. The fact that he can criticize Trump from inside the orbit without losing access suggests he's less captured than the others.
